questions.question: Why does glass refract violet light more strongly than red?
questions.solution: Refractive index depends on wavelength: shorter wavelengths interact more strongly with the glass's electrons, so n_violet > n_red. Since Snell's law uses n, violet bends more at every surface. Dispersion is the wavelength-dependence of refractive index — not a property of the prism's shape.

questions.question: Explain how a rainbow forms using dispersion plus internal reflection, and why it appears at 42°.
questions.solution: Sunlight enters a raindrop, disperses (violet bends more), reflects once off the back, and exits further dispersed. The geometry concentrates each colour into a cone at a specific angle from the antisolar point — red at ~42°, violet at ~40° — so each observer sees their own rainbow. Dispersion + one internal reflection + the 42° cone is the mechanism.

questions.question: What distinguishes the secondary rainbow from the primary in formation and appearance?
questions.solution: Secondary: TWO internal reflections inside the drop (instead of one), so more light is lost — it is fainter; extra reflection reverses the colour order (red inside) and the exit angle is larger (~51°). Primary: one reflection, brighter, red outside. Reflection count drives both brightness and colour order.

questions.question: A prism produces a spectrum 2° wide for white light. What is angular dispersion, and what would double the prism angle do to it?
questions.solution: Angular dispersion = δ_violet − δ_red = the angular spread between extreme colours (2° here). It grows with the prism's refracting angle A and the material's dispersive power — doubling A roughly doubles each colour's deviation and hence the spread. Dispersion is engineered via angle and material.

questions.question: Why does a wide slit produce a spectrum where the colours overlap at the edges (impure spectrum), and how is a pure spectrum obtained?
questions.solution: Each point of a wide slit forms its own spectrum, and neighbouring points' spectra overlap — colours mix at the boundaries. A pure spectrum needs each colour's image as a separate sharp line: use a NARROW slit, so each point's spectrum is thin and the colours separate cleanly. Slit width controls spectral purity.

questions.concept: Why the sky is blue but sunsets are red
questions.question: The same scattering process makes the noon sky blue and a sunset red. Why the two colours?
questions.solution: Rayleigh scattering intensity goes as 1/λ⁴, so short wavelengths scatter far more strongly. Looking away from the sun you see scattered blue light (blue sky). Looking THROUGH a long atmospheric path at sunset, the blue has been scattered out of the beam, leaving the transmitted red/orange. One law, two viewing geometries.

questions.concept: Why a rainbow is a circle of colour
questions.question: Rainbows form at about 42° from the antisolar point and are ordered red-outside. Why these particular numbers and that ordering?
questions.solution: Light entering a spherical drop refracts, reflects internally once and refracts out, with deviation depending on wavelength; the intensity piles up near the minimum-deviation angle, ~42° for red and ~40° for violet. Red deviates less, so it emerges at the larger angle — the outer edge of the arc. Colour order and angular radius both come from the drop's geometry, not from the sky's decoration.

questions.concept: Why chromatic aberration happens in a lens
questions.question: A simple convex lens gives violet and red images at slightly different places. Why, and how does an achromatic doublet fix it?
questions.solution: Focal length depends on μ, and μ depends on wavelength, so each colour focuses at a different point — chromatic aberration. An achromatic doublet pairs a converging crown element with a diverging flint element whose dispersion nearly cancels the crown's, bringing two wavelengths to a common focus. You cannot remove dispersion with one glass; you cancel it with a second of different dispersion.
